transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doctor. I, uh... well, I guess I'm here because things have been feeling incredibly complicated lately, especially around my work. I'm a personal financial advisor here in Cincinnati, and a huge part of my job—probably way more than most people realize when they think of finance—is networking. You know, attending galas, mixing with the arts and finance crowds, building trust with potential clients. It's a very specific, tight-knit kind of ecosystem. 

But for a while now, I’ve been completely convinced that certain people in those specific circles are... well, they're quietly tracking me. They are keeping tabs on exactly which clients I meet with. And it’s not just a passing feeling, it’s like they’re actively sending me these little signals to let me know they know what I'm doing. It happens with the invitations I receive to certain functions, or suddenly the panel topics at these networking dinners will align perfectly with a private portfolio conversation I literally just had with a client. Even down to who sits near me at these events—it's always specific people, positioned in a way that feels incredibly deliberate, like they are trying to box me in or send a message. 

And I know how it sounds, I really do. I keep trying to rationalize it. I tell myself, you know, maybe it could just be a coincidence, because Cincinnati can feel like a really small town when you get into these high-net-worth circles and everyone knows everyone. But... I just can't really let it go. I spend hours analyzing every interaction, every seating chart, every event itinerary, trying to figure out what they want from me or why they're doing this, and it's just becoming exhausting to deal with on top of my actual job.
When you say these people are tracking you and sending signals, do you think they're trying to harm you or damage your career, or are you less sure about what their ultimate goal is?

See, that is exactly the question, isn't it? That's the part that literally keeps me up at night. I just... I really don't know. If I had a clear idea of what they actually wanted, I feel like I could at least form a strategy, you know? Like, if they want to poach my top clients, okay, I can play defense. I can tighten up my relationships, make some calls, secure my book of business. But I am just completely in the dark about what their endgame is here. 

I mean, I've spent hours—literally hours, sitting in my office after everyone else has gone home for the day—just running through every possible scenario in my head. Is it professional sabotage? Are they trying to make me look incompetent or unstable so they can swoop in and take over my accounts? Or is it just some kind of twisted psychological game? Like, maybe they just want to see if I'll crack under the pressure. 

I remember last Thursday, I was at this big gallery opening in Mount Adams—one of those mandatory mingling things—and I spent the entire evening just trying to read the room, trying to figure out the *why* behind it all. I was watching this one guy from a competing boutique firm, and he kept glancing over at me while he was talking to one of the event organizers, and I just kept thinking, 'Is he trying to ruin my career right now? Or is he just trying to intimidate me so I'll mess up on my own?' I go back and forth on it a hundred times a day. It's like trying to put together a 10,000-piece puzzle where you don't have the picture on the box and you're pretty sure half the pieces are missing. 

So, no, I... I really don't know if they want to actively harm me or if they're just messing with my head. I just know they're doing *something*, they're definitely coordinating it, and honestly, not knowing their actual goal is probably the most exhausting part of this whole ordeal. It just leaves your mind to wander to the worst possible conclusions, you know?
Have you ever heard voices or seen things that other people around you didn't seem to notice or hear?

No, I... I haven't experienced anything like that. I mean, I know what you're getting at, like hallucinations or whatever, right? But no, it's not like that at all. It's not like I'm sitting in my office hearing a disembodied voice telling me to sell off a client's tech stocks or something crazy. And I'm not seeing shadow people in the corners of the networking events. 

Everything I'm seeing is real. The people are real people in my industry. The guy I mentioned at the gallery in Mount Adams—he's a real guy, he works for a firm downtown, I could pull up his LinkedIn right now and show you his face. The seating charts, the panel topics, the emails... they are all physical, real things that anyone else could look at. 

The issue isn't that I'm seeing things that aren't there. It's that I'm seeing the connections between the things that *are* there. It's the pattern. It's the intent behind it all. Like, if you were at that gallery, you would have seen that guy looking over at me, too. You just might not have realized *why* he was doing it, or how it connected to the conversation I had with a client three days prior. But my senses are completely fine. I'm not hearing whispers or seeing visions or anything like that. It's all entirely rooted in reality, which is honestly what makes it so impossible to just brush off. If I was just hearing voices, maybe I could convince myself it was all in my head, you know? But this... this is all actually happening right in front of me.

When you think about these people tracking you and coordinating these signals, do you ever have moments where you genuinely doubt whether it's really happening, or are you completely certain that this is definitely occurring?

Like I was trying to explain before, I do try to rationalize it. I really, really do. I mean, I have a degree in finance, my entire career is built on analyzing data and probabilities, so I’m trained to look for logical explanations. There are definitely moments—usually when I’m at home, away from the office, maybe just having a coffee on a Sunday morning—where I’ll sit there and try to force myself to step back. I’ll think, 'Okay, come on. Is the Cincinnati arts and finance community really organizing their entire event schedules around you?' I try to tell myself it could just be a coincidence. I'll literally say it out loud to myself just to see how it sounds. 

But then... then Monday rolls around. Or I check my email and get the next batch of invitations. And the doubt just... it completely evaporates, because the math doesn't add up for it to be random. How many times can something be a coincidence before it's a statistical impossibility, you know? Like, if I get an invitation to a highly exclusive dinner, and the panel topic is exactly—and I mean conceptually identical to—the niche portfolio strategy I was just discussing with a high-net-worth client behind closed doors... how do I ignore that? 

And then I actually get to the dinner, and I look at the seating arrangements, and I look at who sits near me, and it's the exact same people who were hovering around at the last gallery opening. It's always these specific people in those arts and finance circles. 

So, do I have moments of doubt? I try to. I really try, because honestly, it would be a massive relief if I was just overthinking things. It would be fantastic if I could just go to a networking mixer, drink a glass of wine, and not worry about it. I'll even sit in my car before going into a venue and give myself a whole pep talk about how it's all just random chance. But the second I walk in and see the signals they're sending me in real time... I am completely convinced all over again that they are quietly tracking which clients I meet with. I just can't really let it go. When you see it happening over and over, the coordination is just too deliberate to genuinely believe it's anything else.

Over the past few weeks or months, have there been any days where you felt completely convinced this tracking was happening, and then other days where you weren't so sure, or has it been pretty consistently the same level of certainty throughout?

Well, like I was saying, the certainty kind of ebbs and flows depending on if I'm sitting alone in my house or if I'm actually out at an event, but the overall situation... the whole ordeal with them tracking my client meetings and sending me these signals? That's been going on for, let's see, about two months now. 

I know exactly when it started, actually. It was right around the end of Q3. We were doing the quarterly reviews, and I had this massive push to rebalance some portfolios for a few of my older clients—mostly retirees, you know, shifting them into more conservative municipal bonds, really standard stuff but time-consuming. And that was... yeah, that was exactly two months ago, mid-to-late September. That’s when I first noticed the shift in the atmosphere. I went to a charity gala downtown—the one for the symphony, I think it was—and that was the very first time I saw a seating arrangement that just perfectly mirrored the exact tier list of my top clients. 

At first, you know, week one, week two of this... I was definitely more in that 'maybe I'm not so sure' camp. I was brushing it off, telling myself I just needed a vacation or that the quarter-end stress was getting to me, because Q3 is always a nightmare. I would have days where I completely dismissed it. But then, as the weeks went on, through October and now into this month, the certainty just... it locked in. 

So over this two-month period, it's gone from a sort of creeping, easily dismissible suspicion to this daily reality. Every single week for eight weeks, I've had to navigate this. Two months of constantly looking over my shoulder at networking events, analyzing every conversation, trying to figure out how they know who I'm meeting with behind closed doors. It's exhausting. I mean, think about doing your job for two solid months where every time you close your office door to have a private, confidential financial discussion, you know someone is somehow keeping tabs on it and planning to signal you about it at the next mixer. 

So, yeah, the level of certainty has definitely solidified over these last two months. Even if I have those brief Sunday morning moments I mentioned where I try to talk myself out of it, the sheer volume of evidence over the last eight weeks just brings me right back to being absolutely certain it's happening. It's just been a relentless two months, honestly.

You mentioned that over these two months the certainty has solidified. But I want to be very specific: have there been any days in these past two months—even just a day or two—where you woke up and the tracking and signals just weren't on your mind at all, where you felt like it might not actually be happening? Or has it been something you've been thinking about every single day for the full eight weeks?

Well, to be completely honest with you, and I know I’ve been talking in circles about this a bit, but... no. There really hasn't been a single day where it’s just completely off my radar. Not one full day. I mean, I came in to see you specifically because of how relentless this whole thing is. For a while now, like I’ve been saying, I’ve been utterly convinced that these certain people in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati are quietly tracking which clients I meet with, and it's just... it's always there. It permeates everything I do.

Even if I don't have a specific networking event on the calendar for that day, the infrastructure of it all is still sitting right there in my inbox, or on my desk. Like, say it's a Tuesday and I don't have a gallery opening or a charity dinner to go to. I might wake up and think, 'Okay, today is just about the numbers, just me and the spreadsheets, I'm not going to think about them.' But then the mail comes, or I get a notification on my phone, and it’s another one of those targeted invitations. Or I'll see an updated itinerary for a local conference next month, and the panel topics have magically shifted again to perfectly align with a confidential conversation I had the day before. 

So, even when I actively try to force myself to take a mental day off from it... I just can't. I'll sit there at my desk and tell myself, 'Hey, maybe it's just a coincidence that they changed the keynote speaker to cover tax-deferred municipal trusts right after I spent three hours discussing that exact thing with a major client.' I really, really try to tell myself it could just be a coincidence, just a fluke of the industry. But I can’t really let it go. The thought is always hovering right there at the back of my mind, every single day. 

Because how could I just forget about it? My entire livelihood depends on protecting my clients' privacy, and knowing that these people are sending me little signals through the invitations, the panel topics, even who sits near me at these events... it makes it impossible to just turn my brain off. I'm constantly analyzing it, Monday through Sunday, for the whole eight weeks. There's just no off switch for it, no matter how hard I try to ignore it.

In these past two months, have there been any moments—even brief ones, like an hour or two—where you completely stopped believing this was happening and thought 'I was wrong about all of this,' before the conviction came back? Or has your belief stayed at that same solid level of certainty the whole time?

I know we keep circling back to this, and I feel like a broken record, but... no, not even for an hour. I mean, I really wish I could give you a different answer. I wish I could say there was a whole afternoon where I just laughed it off and thought, 'Wow, I was totally wrong about all of this, I'm just being paranoid.' But it just doesn't work that way. 

Like I’ve been trying to explain, the reason I came in to see you in the first place is exactly because of how inescapable this whole situation is. For a while now, I’ve just been so absolutely convinced that these certain people in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati are quietly tracking which clients I meet with. And it's not just some vague, abstract feeling that I can just turn off for a couple of hours while I watch a movie or go to the gym. It's right in my face. They are constantly sending me these little signals through the invitations I get, the specific panel topics they choose, even who sits near me at these events. 

So, if I try to take an hour and say, 'Okay, I'm completely wrong, none of this is real,' my brain just immediately starts running through the data. I'll think about the last charity dinner, or the last gallery opening, and the sheer mathematical improbability of it all. I'll sit there and tell myself it could just be a coincidence—I really, actively try to force myself to believe that it's all just random chance and I'm making connections where there aren't any. I'll try to be the rational financial advisor who only looks at hard facts. 

But I can’t really let it go. The conviction always comes rushing right back within minutes, definitely not hours. Because the moment I try to let it go, I remember the exact wording on an invitation, or how a panel topic perfectly matched a confidential portfolio strategy I just discussed behind closed doors. You just... you can't unsee that kind of coordination once you've noticed it. It's like trying to un-solve a puzzle. So, no, the certainty hasn't ever fully dropped away to the point where I genuinely thought I was wrong. It's just always there, anchoring me to this reality, no matter how hard I try to rationalize my way out of it.

We were doing the quarterly reviews, and I had this massive push to rebalance some portfolios for a few of my older clients—mostly retirees, you know, shifting them into more conservative municipal bonds, really standard stuff but time-consuming. And that was... yeah, that was exactly two months ago, mid-to-late September. That’s when I first noticed the shift in the atmosphere. I went to a charity gala downtown—the one for the symphony, I think it was—and that was the very first time I saw a seating arrangement that just perfectly mirrored the exact tier list of my top clients. 

At first, you know, week one, week two of this... I was definitely more in that 'maybe I'm not so sure' camp. I was brushing it off, telling myself I just needed a vacation or that the quarter-end stress was getting to me, because Q3 is always a nightmare. I would have days where I completely dismissed it. But then, as the weeks went on, through October and now into this month, the certainty just... it locked in. 

So over this two-month period, it's gone from a sort of creeping, easily dismissible suspicion to this daily reality. Every single week for eight weeks, I've had to navigate this. Two months of constantly looking over my shoulder at networking events, analyzing every conversation, trying to figure out how they know who I'm meeting with behind closed doors. It's exhausting. I mean, think about doing your job for two solid months where every time you close your office door to have a private, confidential financial discussion, you know someone is somehow keeping tabs on it and planning to signal you about it at the next mixer. 

So, yeah, the level of certainty has definitely solidified over these last two months. Even if I have those brief Sunday morning moments I mentioned where I try to talk myself out of it, the sheer volume of evidence over the last eight weeks just brings me right back to being absolutely certain it's happening. It's just been a relentless two months, honestly.

patient.answer:
Well, to be completely honest with you, and I know I’ve been talking in circles about this a bit, but... no. There really hasn't been a single day where it’s just completely off my radar. Not one full day. I mean, I came in to see you specifically because of how relentless this whole thing is. For a while now, like I’ve been saying, I’ve been utterly convinced that these certain people in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati are quietly tracking which clients I meet with, and it's just... it's always there. It permeates everything I do.

Even if I don't have a specific networking event on the calendar for that day, the infrastructure of it all is still sitting right there in my inbox, or on my desk. Like, say it's a Tuesday and I don't have a gallery opening or a charity dinner to go to. I might wake up and think, 'Okay, today is just about the numbers, just me and the spreadsheets, I'm not going to think about them.' But then the mail comes, or I get a notification on my phone, and it’s another one of those targeted invitations. Or I'll see an updated itinerary for a local conference next month, and the panel topics have magically shifted again to perfectly align with a confidential conversation I had the day before. 

So, even when I actively try to force myself to take a mental day off from it... I just can't. I'll sit there at my desk and tell myself, 'Hey, maybe it's just a coincidence that they changed the keynote speaker to cover tax-deferred municipal trusts right after I spent three hours discussing that exact thing with a major client.' I really, really try to tell myself it could just be a coincidence, just a fluke of the industry. But I can’t really let it go. The thought is always hovering right there at the back of my mind, every single day. 

Because how could I just forget about it? My entire livelihood depends on protecting my clients' privacy, and knowing that these people are sending me little signals through the invitations, the panel topics, even who sits near me at these events... it makes it impossible to just turn my brain off. I'm constantly analyzing it, Monday through Sunday, for the whole eight weeks. There's just no off switch for it, no matter how hard I try to ignore it.

doctor.question: In these past two months, have there been any moments—even brief ones, like an hour or two—where you completely stopped believing this was happening and thought 'I was wrong about all of this,' before the conviction came back? Or has your belief stayed at that same solid level of certainty the whole time?

patient.answer:
I know we keep circling back to this, and I feel like a broken record, but... no, not even for an hour. I mean, I really wish I could give you a different answer. I wish I could say there was a whole afternoon where I just laughed it off and thought, 'Wow, I was totally wrong about all of this, I'm just being paranoid.' But it just doesn't work that way. 

Like I’ve been trying to explain, the reason I came in to see you in the first place is exactly because of how inescapable this whole situation is. For a while now, I’ve just been so absolutely convinced that these certain people in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati are quietly tracking which clients I meet with. And it's not just some vague, abstract feeling that I can just turn off for a couple of hours while I watch a movie or go to the gym. It's right in my face. They are constantly sending me these little signals through the invitations I get, the specific panel topics they choose, even who sits near me at these events. 

So, if I try to take an hour and say, 'Okay, I'm completely wrong, none of this is real,' my brain just immediately starts running through the data. I'll think about the last charity dinner, or the last gallery opening, and the sheer mathematical improbability of it all. I'll sit there and tell myself it could just be a coincidence—I really, actively try to force myself to believe that it's all just random chance and I'm making connections where there aren't any. I'll try to be the rational financial advisor who only looks at hard facts. 

But I can’t really let it go. The conviction always comes rushing right back within minutes, definitely not hours. Because the moment I try to let it go, I remember the exact wording on an invitation, or how a panel topic perfectly matched a confidential portfolio strategy I just discussed behind closed doors. You just... you can't unsee that kind of coordination once you've noticed it. It's like trying to un-solve a puzzle. So, no, the certainty hasn't ever fully dropped away to the point where I genuinely thought I was wrong. It's just always there, anchoring me to this reality, no matter how hard I try to rationalize my way out of it.

inference.note: Patient demonstrates fixed, non-bizarre delusions of reference (tracking and coordinated signals) that have persisted for 2 months with complete certainty and no periods of doubt lasting even brief intervals. Denies hallucinations. Functioning remains relatively intact (still working). This is consistent with F22.0 (Delusional disorder, erotomanic type is ruled out given the nature of delusions; persecutory type fits best). F22.9 can be removed as the specific type is now identifiable.
